claim: miR-965 is located in the first intron of the kismet gene.
source: The miR-965 microRNA is located in the first intron of the kismet gene (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in text and shown in Figure 1A diagram

claim: kismet and miR-965 are transcribed in the same direction.
source: kismet and miR-965 are transcribed in the same direction.
evidence: Directly stated in the text

claim: A series of P-element insertional mutants near the first exon of the kismet gene reduced the level of mature miR-965 miRNA.
source: Quantitative PCR showed that a series of P-element insertional mutants near the first exon of the kismet gene reduced the level of mature miR-965 miRNA, suggesting that kismet and miR-965 arise from a single transcription unit (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: kismet and miR-965 arise from a single transcription unit.
source: Quantitative PCR showed that a series of P-element insertional mutants near the first exon of the kismet gene reduced the level of mature miR-965 miRNA, suggesting that kismet and miR-965 arise from a single transcription unit (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that kismet P-element mutants reduce miR-965 levels

claim: The w+KO1 mutant allele was made by replacing miR-965 with a mini-white reporter gene flanked by LoxP sites.
source: One mutant allele was made by homologous recombination using the pw25 vector (Gong and Golic, 2003). In this allele, the genomic region containing the miRNA hairpin was replaced by a mini-white reporter gene flanked by LoxP sites (Figure 1A, w+KO1).
evidence: Described in text and shown in Figure 1A diagram

claim: Cre-mediated excision of the LoxP-flanked mini-white cassette produced the KO1 allele.
source: Cre-mediated excision of the LoxP-flanked mini-white cassette produced the KO1 allele, in which the miRNA was replaced by a single LoxP site (Figure 1A, w-KO1).
evidence: Described in text and shown in Figure 1A

claim: The KO2 allele was made by Cre-mediated excision of the LoxP flanked mini-white reporter.
source: The KO2 allele was made by Cre-mediated excision of the LoxP flanked mini-white reporter (Figure 1A, w-KO2).
evidence: Described in text and shown in Figure 1A

claim: Deletion of the miRNA was verified by quantitative miRNA PCR in animals heteroallelic for KO1/KO2 and for the KO2 allele in trans to Df(2L)ED19.
source: Deletion of the miRNA was verified by quantitative miRNA PCR in animals heteroallelic for the mini-white deleted versions of KO1/KO2 and for the KO2 allele in trans to Df(2L)ED19, a chromosomal deletion that uncovers the kismet gene (Figure 1B).
evidence: Verified by quantitative miRNA PCR data shown in Figure 1B

claim: RMCE was used to replace the mini-white cassette with a fragment containing the miR-965 hairpin to produce a genetic rescue allele.
source: To produce a genetic rescue allele, we used RMCE to replace the mini-white cassette with a fragment containing the miR-965 hairpin (Figure 1A, 965-Rescue).
evidence: Described in text and shown in Figure 1A

claim: miR-965 expression was restored to normal levels in the 965-Rescue allele.
source: miR-965 expression was restored to normal levels in the 965-Rescue allele (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown by quantitative miRNA PCR data in Figure 1B

claim: A PCR product of normal size was produced in RNA isolated from miR-965w-KO1/miR-965w-KO2 and miR-965w-KO2/Df animals, indicating normal splicing of the first kismet intron.
source: Figure 1C shows RT-PCR to assess splicing of the first kismet intron. A PCR product of normal size was produced in RNA isolated from miR-965w-KO1/miR-965w-KO2 and miR-965w-KO2/Df animals.
evidence: RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C

claim: kismet transcript levels were not reduced in the miR-965w-KO1/miR-965w-KO2 flies compared to controls.
source: kismet transcript levels were not reduced in the miR-965w-KO1/miR-965w-KO2 flies compared to controls, indicating that splicing of intron 1 was not impaired in these mutants.
evidence: Confirmed by quantitative PCR shown in Figure 1D

claim: The miR-965w-KO1 and miR-965w-KO2 mutant alleles were viable in trans to kismet1, a lethal allele.
source: Genetic complementation tests also showed that the miR-965w-KO1 and miR-965w-KO2 mutant alleles were viable in trans to kismet1, a lethal allele, as well as in trans to Df(2L)ED19, which removes kismet.
evidence: Genetic complementation test results

claim: The miR-965w-KO1 and miR-965w-KO2 mutant alleles were viable in trans to Df(2L)ED19, which removes kismet.
source: Genetic complementation tests also showed that the miR-965w-KO1 and miR-965w-KO2 mutant alleles were viable in trans to kismet1, a lethal allele, as well as in trans to Df(2L)ED19, which removes kismet.
evidence: Genetic complementation test results

claim: The mini-white excised mutant miR-965w-KO1 and miR-965w-KO2 alleles do not compromise kismet gene function.
source: Together, these data provide evidence that the mini-white excised mutant miR-965w-KO1 and miR-965w-KO2 alleles do not compromise kismet gene function.
evidence: Based on RT-PCR, quantitative PCR, and genetic complementation data

claim: Mutants lacking miR-965 had only minor effects on survival during development.
source: Mutants lacking miR-965 had only minor effects on survival during development.
evidence: Observation from developmental studies

claim: Mutant adults appeared to be morphologically normal with the exception of defects in abdominal segmentation.
source: Mutant adults appeared to be morphologically normal with the exception of defects in abdominal segmentation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Morphological observation shown in Figure 1E

claim: The predominant defect in miR-965 mutants was a dorsal gap in one or more abdominal segments, in some cases leading to segment fusion.
source: Among the affected individuals, the predominant defect was a dorsal gap in one or more abdominal segments, in some cases leading to segment fusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Phenotypic observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Formation of ectopic bristles associated with a polarity defect was observed in ∼15% of affected individuals.
source: In addition, formation of ectopic bristles associated with a polarity defect was observed in ∼15% of affected individuals (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Quantified phenotypic observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Polarity reversal was always accompanied by a gap or segment fusion phenotype.
source: Polarity reversal was always accompanied by a gap or segment fusion phenotype.
evidence: Observation from phenotypic analysis

claim: The abdominal segmentation defects were rescued by restoring miRNA expression using the miR-965 RMCE rescue allele.
source: These defects were rescued by restoring miRNA expression using the miR-965 RMCE rescue allele (Figure 1E).
evidence: Rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1E

claim: miR-965 sensor GFP levels were lower in the histoblast nests compared to the adjacent larval cells.
source: miR-965 sensor GFP levels were lower in the histoblast nests, compared to the adjacent larval cells, particularly in the histoblast cells near the edge of the nests (Figure 2).
evidence: Sensor transgene data shown in Figure 2

claim: The reduced GFP level in the histoblasts is due to miR-965-mediated repression.
source: This difference was lost when the sensor was introduced into the miR-965 mutant background, providing evidence that the reduced GFP level in the histoblasts is due to miR-965-mediated repression (Figure 2).
evidence: Sensor transgene data in mutant background shown in Figure 2

claim: Histoblasts are small diploid cells, easily distinguishable from the large polyploid larval epidermal cells (LEC) that surround them.
source: Histoblasts are small diploid cells, easily distinguishable from the large polyploid larval epidermal cells (LEC) that surround them.
evidence: Established knowledge about histoblast cell characteristics

claim: Histoblasts are specified in the embryo and lie quiescent throughout larval development.
source: Histoblasts are specified in the embryo and lie quiescent throughout larval development (Guerra et al., 1973; Simcox et al., 1991).
evidence: Cited from previous studies

claim: There are four pairs of histoblast nests in each segment.
source: There are four pairs of histoblast nests in each segment, which merge to assemble the adult abdominal epidermis (Madhavan and Schneiderman, 1977).
evidence: Cited from previous study

claim: The anterior and posterior dorsal histoblast nests give rise to the external dorsal cuticle of the abdominal segments (tergites).
source: The anterior and posterior dorsal histoblast nests give rise to the external dorsal cuticle of the abdominal segments (tergites), while the ventral pair give rise to the ventral cuticle (sternites).
evidence: Established knowledge about histoblast development

claim: During larval stages, histoblasts are arrested in the G2 phase of the cell cycle.
source: During larval stages, histoblasts are arrested in the G2 phase of the cell cycle.
evidence: Established knowledge about histoblast cell cycle

claim: At pupariation, an ecdysone pulse triggers the expression of string (cdc25), which activates cyclin/CDK and pushes the histoblasts into rapid proliferation.
source: At pupariation, an ecdysone pulse triggers the expression of string (cdc25), which activates cyclin/CDK and pushes the histoblasts into rapid proliferation (Edgar and O'Farrell, 1990; Gautier et al., 1991).
evidence: Cited from previous studies

claim: The proliferative phase is divided into two stages with distinct features.
source: The proliferative phase is divided into two stages with distinct features (Madhavan and Madhavan, 1980; Ninov et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from previous studies

claim: The early 'division phase' is characterized by rapid and synchronous cell division without intervening G2 phases to allow for cell growth.
source: The early 'division phase' is characterized by rapid and synchronous cell division without intervening G2 phases to allow for cell growth.
evidence: Established knowledge about histoblast division phase

claim: Cells double in number and decrease in size with each division during the early division phase, with little change in the size of the nests.
source: Cells double in number and decrease in size with each division, with little change in the size of the nests.
evidence: Established knowledge about histoblast division phase

claim: The early division phase is followed by a phase of slower division, from 15–40 hr of pupal development, in which proliferation is accompanied by longer intervening gap phases to allow cell growth.
source: This is followed by a phase of slower division, from 15–40 hr of pupal development, in which proliferation is accompanied by longer intervening gap phases to allow cell growth.
evidence: Established knowledge about histoblast growth phase

claim: During the growth phase, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and Insulin receptor/PI3K-signaling coordinate the growth of cells with proliferation.
source: During this phase, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and Insulin receptor/PI3K- signaling coordinate the growth of cells with proliferation (Ninov et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from previous study

claim: During the growth phase, the histoblast nests begin to spread to replace the LEC.
source: During this phase, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and Insulin receptor/PI3K- signaling coordinate the growth of cells with proliferation (Ninov et al., 2009). During the growth phase, the histoblast nests begin to spread to replace the LEC.
evidence: Established knowledge about histoblast development

claim: The expansion of the histoblast nests by cell migration is accompanied by programmed cell death, so that larval cells are replaced by the expanding histoblast population to maintain integrity of the epithelium.
source: The expansion of the histoblast nests by cell migration is accompanied by programmed cell death, so that larval cells are replaced by the expanding histoblast population to maintain integrity of the epithelium (Bischoff and Cseresnyes, 2009; Nakajima et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from previous studies

claim: In the controls, cells became smaller and the number of cells doubled after each division during the early division phase.
source: In the controls, cells became smaller and the number of cells doubled after each division (Video 1).
evidence: Observation from time-lapse video shown in Video 1

claim: The pattern of synchronous division was perturbed in the miR-965 mutant.
source: This pattern of synchronous division was perturbed in the miR-965 mutant.

claim: Asynchronous division of miR-965 mutant histoblasts resulted in the presence of cells of different sizes.
source: Asynchronous division of miR-965 mutant histoblasts resulted in the presence of cells of different sizes (Figure 3A, Video 2).
evidence: Observation from time-lapse video and images shown in Figure 3A and Video 2

claim: In the miR-965 mutant, a subset of histoblast nuclei became pyknotic, fragmented and disappeared, indicating cell death.
source: In the mutant, a subset of histoblast nuclei became pyknotic, fragmented and disappeared, indicating cell death (Video 3).
evidence: Observation from time-lapse video shown in Video 3

claim: Cell death was rare during the early division phase in the control samples.
source: Cell death was rare during this phase in the control samples.
evidence: Observation from time-lapse videos

claim: Synchronous division was restored and cell death was suppressed in the miR-965-rescue allele.
source: Synchronous division was restored and cell death was suppressed in the miR-965-rescue allele (Figure 3A, Video 4).

claim: The rate of histoblast nest expansion was slower in the miR-965 mutant, compared to the controls.
source: Subsequently, the rate of histoblast nest expansion was slower in the miR-965 mutant, compared to the controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: Observation from time-lapse videos shown in Figure 3B

claim: The average speed of migration of third and fourth histoblast nests in the control samples was 15 µm/hr.
source: The average speed of migration of third and fourth histoblast nests in the control samples was 15 µm/hr, compare with ∼6.5 µm/hr in the mutant.

claim: The average speed of migration of third and fourth histoblast nests in the miR-965 mutant was ∼6.5 µm/hr.
source: The average speed of migration of third and fourth histoblast nests in the control samples was 15 µm/hr, compare with ∼6.5 µm/hr in the mutant.
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse videos shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The rate of nest expansion was increased to 12–14 µm/hr by restoring miR-965 expression with the rescue allele.
source: The rate of nest expansion was increased to 12–14 µm/hr by restoring miR-965 expression with the rescue allele the miR-965 mutant background (Video 7).
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse video shown in Video 7

claim: In miR-965 mutants, some larval epidermal cells were still present in the nests, suggesting a failure to eliminate LECs in the mutant.
source: In miR-965 mutants, we observed that some of these cells were still present in the nests, suggesting a failure to eliminate LECs in the mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Delayed expansion of the histoblast nests, combined with the persistence of LECs, is likely to be responsible for the gaps observed in adult abdominal segments.
source: Delayed expansion of the histoblast nests, combined with the persistence of LECs, is likely to be responsible for the gaps observed in adult abdominal segments.

claim: miR-965 is predicted to target 69 genes.
source: miR-965 is predicted to target 69 genes (www.targetscan.org).
evidence: Prediction from TargetScan database

claim: Only string and wingless (wg) mRNAs were upregulated in RNA isolated from miR-965 mutant pupae among the tested candidate targets.
source: Of these, only string and wingless (wg) mRNAs were upregulated in RNA isolated from miR-965 mutant pupae, and were also restored to near normal levels in the rescued mutant (Figure 4A,B), as would be expected for functional miRNA targets.

claim: string and wingless mRNAs were restored to near normal levels in the rescued mutant.
source: Of these, only string and wingless (wg) mRNAs were upregulated in RNA isolated from miR-965 mutant pupae, and were also restored to near normal levels in the rescued mutant (Figure 4A,B), as would be expected for functional miRNA targets.

claim: miR-965 expression reduced wg 3′UTR reporter activity.
source: miR-965 expression reduced wg 3′UTR reporter activity, and this regulation was lost in the wg UTR reporter mutated to disrupt pairing with the miRNA seed sequence (Figure 4C, mutated residues shown in red).

claim: Regulation of the wg 3′UTR reporter by miR-965 was lost when the reporter was mutated to disrupt pairing with the miRNA seed sequence.
source: miR-965 expression reduced wg 3′UTR reporter activity, and this regulation was lost in the wg UTR reporter mutated to disrupt pairing with the miRNA seed sequence (Figure 4C, mutated residues shown in red).

claim: miR-965 expression reduced expression of the string 3′UTR luciferase reporter.
source: miR-965 expression also reduced expression of the string 3′UTR luciferase reporter (Figure 4D).

claim: Mutation of the predicted target site to disrupt seed pairing partially offset regulation of the string 3′UTR luciferase reporter.
source: Mutation of the predicted target site to disrupt seed pairing partially offset regulation of the string 3′UTR luciferase reporter (Figure 4D, mutated residues in red).
evidence: Luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4D

claim: More extensive mutation to disrupt both sites in the string 3′UTR further compromised regulation by miR-965.
source: More extensive mutation to disrupt both sites further compromised regulation by miR-965 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4D

claim: miR-965 can regulate expression of string and wg.
source: These findings provide evidence that miR-965 can regulate expression of string and wg.

source: esg-Gal4 driven expression of a UAS-string transgene produced abdominal segment gaps, segment fusion and polarity reversal phenotypes, similar to those observed in the miR-965 mutant (Figure 5A Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Expansion of the string-overexpressing histoblast nests was slowed, and the histoblasts were unable to fully replace the LECs.
source: Expansion of the string-overexpressing histoblast nests was slowed, and the histoblasts were unable to fully replace the LECs (Figure 5—figure supplements 2, 3, Video 9), similar to what was observed in miR-965 mutants.

claim: string overexpression was sufficient to reproduce the miR-965 mutant phenotype.
source: Thus, string overexpression was sufficient to reproduce the miR-965 mutant phenotype.

claim: Lowering string activity suppressed the asynchronous division phenotype of the miR-965 mutant.

claim: Lowering string activity suppressed the slow cell migration phenotype of the miR-965 mutant.

claim: Wingless protein (Wg) is expressed in the anterior dorsal histoblast nests, during their growth and migration.

source: These experiments provide evidence that overexpression of string and wg each contribute to the miR-965 mutant histoblast phenotypes.

claim: RNAi-mediated depletion of EcR mRNA led to reduced string mRNA levels in RNA samples isolated from early pupae.

claim: EcR binding sites have been identified near the host gene, kismet.
